newsitem.title: USA: African official says U.S. business is welcome.
newsitem.headline: African official says U.S. business is welcome.

text.p: A senior Ethiopian official said on Saturday that Africa was rolling out the red carpet for U.S. business and that it would be a mistake to underestimate the potential because of past experience.

In remarks to the opening of a conference sponsored by the Corporate Council on Africa, Deputy Prime Minister Kassu Illala told a gathering of African leaders and U.S. business executives that the continent has changed and cases of political disorder were the exception rather than the rule.

"The overall trend in Africa today is towards democratization and towards the creation of an environment very much conducive to development and to the nurturing of effective business relations with the outside world," he told the delegates.
He said the continent should not be treated by the U.S. business community "on the basis of images that are no longer an accurate reflection of the reality now prevailing in most of Africa."

The meeting of the group in suburban Washington comes just before the semi-annual gathering of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank at which a long awaited new debt relief initiative for very poor countries -- most in Africa -- is expected to go into effect.

Uganda will be the first country to benefit from the plan, although it is expected to be closely followed by the Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso, and Bolivia. Some 33 or the 44 countries that could be eligible are in Africa.

The initiative, which combines the efforts of the IMF, World Bank and the Paris Club of creditor nations, is designed to provide poor countries that persevere with tough economic reforms with debt relief.

While such assistance is critical to help poor countries overwhelmed with debt -- including past loans from the lending agencies themselves -- the meeting of African leaders and the business community underscored the spread of investment interest by the private sector in developing countries around the world.

The meeting of African officials, which ends on Tuesday, will be addressed by First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin. The delegates will also see a video address by President Bill Clinton
This is the first conference of this kind by the corporate council which has was formed in 1992 to help generate activity by the private sector in Africa.
